drhp.business: Karma Energy is engaged in renewable power generation through wind farm development and operation; the Board's report notes the Company is in the field of wind farm development and not manufacturing. It operates wind farms in Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra and sells generation to State Electricity Boards / utilities and, where open access permits, to third parties. The Company has no subsidiaries, associates or joint ventures, and there was no change in the business of the company during the year as compared to the previous year.
drhp.end_markets: State electricity utilities / State Electricity Boards (India)|Third-party open-access power buyers|Tamil Nadu|Maharashtra
drhp.expansion: The annual report discloses no expansion or new capex project. The direction is the opposite: the MD&A states the Company now has about 30.50 MW of power generating wind farms and had closed down loss-making and low-tariff wind farms in Andhra Pradesh and a unit in Tamil Nadu, and that wind mills which have outlived their technical life — where continued operation even with good operation and maintenance may prove uneconomical because tariffs remain fixed with no adjustment for inflation or actual repair and establishment costs — have been retired. litigation.note: The Corporate Governance Report discloses a SEBI adjudication/settlement proceeding over deviations from the Listing Regulations, with a hearing concluded on 13.05.2025 and an order issued on 10th July 2025 imposing a penalty on the Company, which was promptly remitted; it also discloses BSE notices received on 6th April 2026 for non-compliance with Regulation 17(1) of SEBI LODR for the quarters ended 30th September 2024 and 31st December 2024, with penalties since paid. Separately, MD&A describes inordinate delays in adjudication of matters by the Electricity Regulatory Commission, the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity and even High Courts causing acute pressure on the Company, and the Board's report refers to interest on non-payment of D S Metals dues of 2013 from TANGEDCO recorded as an Exceptional Item.

risks.note: MD&A states 'The performance of the Company is directly linked to the Renewable Energy Policies of both Centre and State Governments, effectiveness of Nodal Agencies and formulation of encouraging policies and implementation thereof by State Electricity Regulatory Commissions.' The Company has no control over the single variable that sets its revenue.
risks.risk: Total dependence on renewable-energy policy of Centre and State Governments and on State Electricity Regulatory Commissions

risks.note: MD&A says in many states tariffs 'have not being encouraging' and that tariff remains fixed for many years with no adjustment to inflation or the factual cost of repairs and establishment costs, so ageing wind mills 'may prove uneconomical' even with good operation and maintenance.

MD&A: 'sale to third parties are being discouraged by imposing high open access charges under one pretext or other', which the Company reads as continued regulatory support for conventional energy and which closes off the higher-realisation merchant channel.

MD&A: 'In the wind power business the expenses are more or less fixed, the delayed receipt of generation proceeds necessitate that company has to resort to temporary borrowings to tide over the mismatch. This is also a concern as it has to bear the brunt of finance cost.' Partially mitigated by the Ministry of Power's 'Prapti' portal, which has helped the Company tackle liquidity issues.
risks.risk: Receivable delays from state utilities against a fixed cost base

risks.note: MD&A: 'inordinate delays in adjudication of the matters by Electricity Regulatory Commission, Appellate Tribunal for Electricity and even High courts result in acute pressure on the Company due to huge mismatch in inflow and outflow of funds', and the same delays are 'impeding the future projects'.
risks.risk: Inordinate delays in adjudication by regulators, APTEL and High Courts

risks.note: MD&A repeatedly states that 'present environment in Green Energy is only for Big Players with deep pockets developing in terms of thousands of MW', that such houses can absorb running losses and negotiate better with utilities due to their size, and that many small and medium entities that entered two decades back have closed their units. Karma operates about 30.50 MW.
risks.risk: Sub-scale position in a sector that has consolidated toward large players

risks.note: MD&A's ratio commentary attributes the year's loss and the adverse interest coverage and net profit margin to 'higher Operation and Maintenance Costs, repairs to Wind mills at different sites' despite improved turnover; wind mills that outlived their technical life have had to be retired and units in Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu were closed.
risks.risk: Ageing asset base driving volatile operation, maintenance and repair costs

sk.overview: The DRHP frames the issuer's industry through a CRISIL-commissioned report titled "Assessment of Indian power and renewable energy market" (July 2026). India is described as the third largest producer and consumer of electricity globally, operating under a Centre-State concurrent governance framework (MoP/MNRE/CEA/CERC at the Centre, SERCs and DISCOMs at the state level).
